newsitem.title: UK: Aberfan remembers day when generation wiped out.
newsitem.headline: Aberfan remembers day when generation wiped out.

text.p: Exactly 30 years after a black sea of mud wiped out a generation, the villagers of Aberfan are to commemorate the children they still grieve for.
The bereaved in this tight-knit Welsh mining community are to get together to mark the precise moment when a mountainside collapsed and their lives were blighted for ever.
Monday morning's simple service at 0815 GMT in the village cemetery is for relatives and survivors still psychologically scarred by Britain's worst ever landslide.
Every street, every family was touched by the disaster.
A coal tip, which had been undermined by a natural spring, hurtled down the mountainside on October 21, 1966 and engulfed the village school in millions of tonnes of sludge.
Within minutes, 144 people were dead. Of those, 116 were children. Just 10 children were plucked from the choking black hell by miners scrabbling with their bare hands.
The survivors live in fear of the dark. They are eaten up with guilt about being spared. Their grief and misery were bottled up for years. Showing emotion was frowned upon.

"We had no friends. Our childhood was gone. We had to grow up very very quickly," said Jeff Edwards, a survivor who recalls the day they had just sung the hymn "All Things Bright and Beautiful" at the last school assembly before half-term.
"As children we never got any sympathy. We were always told we were lucky to be alive," said Janett Smart, who now works as a doctor's receptionist.

Gaynor Madgwick, who saw friends choke to death in front of her, opened up the emotional floodgates for her fellow survivors last month by publishing the raw account she wrote as a little girl just four years after the tragedy.
Her poignant words, scribbled in a school exercise book, lay hidden in the family attic for years. She survived but her brother and sister died.

Recalling the nightmare that still haunts her today, she wrote: "I could just see someone's hand through the crack in the wall. I squeezed the hand and pinched it to see if it was alive but I could see that it was dead. For all I knew, it could have been my brother's hand."
Her father, Cliff Minett, is fiercely proud of Gaynor.
"Looking back, if we hadn't the others in the family, we would have given up hope. A lot of people's nerves went to pieces," he said.
"I still get bad days when birthdays come along. We were going to move away but you cannot run. What is the point in running? We stuck it out."
Teacher Howell Williams admitted that he turned to drink afterwards to blot out the horrors. "But that didn't help one iota," he told a BBC documentary on the survivors.
The school football team had just defeated their arch local rivals 3-2 in a thrilling match the day before and the memory of their joy will haunt him forever.
"Every member of that football team died and I survived. It just doesn't make sense. It just doesn't make sense. It is unbelievable," he said of the lost generation.
